title: Qdrant
text: Qdrant is an open-source vector database written in Rust. It stores vectors together with JSON payloads, supports filtering on payload fields during the vector search itself, uses HNSW indexing for approximate nearest-neighbour search, offers quantization to reduce memory, and can run embedded, as a single Docker container, or as a distributed cluster. Payload filtering is useful in RAG systems that need to restrict retrieval by user, document or metadata.

title: Vector databases
text: A vector database stores embeddings and answers nearest-neighbour queries efficiently. Common choices include Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Chroma, FAISS (a library rather than a database) and pgvector in PostgreSQL. The trade-offs are managed versus self-hosted operation, metadata filtering support, hybrid search support, scalability, and operational complexity.

title: HNSW index
text: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a graph-based approximate nearest-neighbour index. It builds layered proximity graphs and searches greedily from the top layer down, giving sub-linear query time with high recall. Parameters such as M and ef control the trade-off between recall, memory and speed.

title: Embeddings
text: Embeddings map text, images or other data to dense vectors so that semantically similar items are close together, usually measured with cosine similarity or dot product. Models such as sentence-transformers produce text embeddings, while CLIP maps images and text into a shared space, which enables cross-modal retrieval.

title: Retrieval-augmented generation
text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves relevant passages from a knowledge base and passes them to a language model as context, so answers are grounded in specific sources rather than only the model's parameters. A typical pipeline is ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, optional re-ranking, prompt construction and generation with citations.

title: Chunking strategies
text: Chunking splits documents into retrievable units. Fixed-size chunks with overlap are simple; structure-aware chunking by headings, sections or tables keeps related content together and improves retrieval precision. Chunks that are too large dilute relevance, chunks that are too small lose context. Storing metadata such as source, page and section enables filtering and citations.

title: Hybrid search
text: Hybrid search combines dense vector retrieval with sparse keyword retrieval such as BM25. Dense retrieval captures meaning and paraphrases; keyword retrieval is precise for exact terms, names, identifiers and rare words. Results are usually merged with reciprocal rank fusion or weighted scores.

title: BM25
text: BM25 is a ranking function for keyword search based on term frequency, inverse document frequency and document length normalisation. It remains a strong baseline and is often combined with vector search in hybrid retrieval.

title: Re-ranking
text: A re-ranker, often a cross-encoder, scores each query-passage pair jointly after a fast first-stage retrieval. It improves precision at the top of the result list at the cost of extra latency, so it is usually applied to a small candidate set.

title: Hallucination and grounding
text: LLMs can produce fluent but unsupported statements, known as hallucinations. Mitigations include retrieval grounding, instructing the model to answer only from provided context, citing sources, verifying generated claims against evidence, constraining output formats and evaluating answers with a separate judge or test set.

title: Evaluating RAG systems
text: RAG systems are evaluated at the retrieval level with metrics such as Recall@K, Precision@K and MRR, and at the answer level for faithfulness to the retrieved context, answer relevance and correctness. Building a labelled set of questions with known supporting passages makes retrieval changes measurable.

title: CLIP
text: CLIP is a model trained with contrastive learning on image-text pairs. It produces image and text embeddings in the same vector space, so a text query can retrieve relevant images and vice versa. It is commonly used for multimodal search and zero-shot image classification.

title: Multimodal RAG
text: Multimodal RAG retrieves across text, images and tables. Approaches include embedding images with a shared text-image model like CLIP, converting images and tables to text descriptions before embedding, and keeping per-modality metadata so the generator can cite the right source type.

title: LangChain
text: LangChain is a framework that provides abstractions for LLM applications, including document loaders, text splitters, retrievers, prompt templates, chains and agents. It speeds up prototyping; some teams replace parts of it with custom code in production for more control over retrieval and prompts.

title: Transformers and attention
text: Transformers process sequences with self-attention, where each token computes weighted interactions with every other token using query, key and value projections. Multi-head attention, positional information and feed-forward layers make up each block. Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length.

title: Fine-tuning vs RAG
text: Fine-tuning changes model weights to teach style, format or domain behaviour; parameter-efficient methods like LoRA train small adapter matrices. RAG injects up-to-date or private knowledge at query time without retraining. Facts that change frequently are usually better served by RAG; consistent behaviour or format by fine-tuning.

title: Prompt engineering
text: Effective prompts state the task, provide relevant context, specify the output format and constraints, and include examples when helpful. For grounded applications, prompts tell the model to answer only from the supplied context and to say when the context is insufficient.

title: Flask
text: Flask is a lightweight Python web framework. It provides routing, request handling and templating with minimal structure, and is extended with libraries for databases, authentication and validation. It is popular for small services and ML model APIs because it is simple to set up.

title: FastAPI
text: FastAPI is a Python web framework built on Starlette and Pydantic. It supports async request handling, automatic request validation from type hints, automatic OpenAPI documentation and WebSockets, which makes it well suited to high-concurrency APIs and streaming responses.

title: Flask vs FastAPI
text: Flask is synchronous by default, minimal and mature. FastAPI is async-first, validates requests with Pydantic type hints and generates OpenAPI docs automatically. FastAPI is often chosen for streaming and high-concurrency I/O, Flask for simple services.

title: REST APIs
text: REST APIs expose resources over HTTP using methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE with meaningful status codes. Good practice includes stateless requests, consistent resource naming, pagination, input validation, versioning and authentication.

title: WebSockets
text: WebSockets provide a persistent, full-duplex connection between client and server over a single TCP connection, which suits real-time features such as live transcripts and token streaming. Applications need reconnection logic, heartbeats and a way to resume state after a disconnect.

title: AWS EC2
text: Amazon EC2 provides resizable virtual machines. Deploying a service on EC2 involves choosing an instance type, configuring security groups, installing the runtime or Docker, and often placing a load balancer and auto-scaling group in front for availability.

title: Core AWS services
text: Common AWS building blocks are EC2 for virtual machines, S3 for object storage, Lambda for serverless functions, RDS for managed relational databases, IAM for access control, CloudWatch for monitoring and API Gateway for managed APIs.

title: Docker
text: Docker packages an application and its dependencies into an image that runs as an isolated container, which makes environments reproducible across development and production. Docker Compose defines multi-container setups such as an API, a database and a cache.

title: Kubernetes
text: Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster: it schedules pods, restarts failed containers, scales replicas, performs rolling updates and provides service discovery and configuration management.

title: CI/CD
text: Continuous integration runs builds and tests automatically on every change; continuous delivery or deployment automates releasing tested builds. Pipelines typically include linting, tests, security scans, image builds and staged deployments.

title: Database indexing
text: An index is a data structure, commonly a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Indexes speed up reads and lookups on filtered or joined columns but add write overhead and storage. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule.

title: Transactions and ACID
text: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Transactions group operations so they succeed or fail together. Isolation levels such as read committed, repeatable read and serializable trade concurrency for protection against anomalies.

title: SQL vs NoSQL
text: Relational databases such as PostgreSQL offer schemas, joins and strong transactional guarantees. NoSQL databases such as MongoDB, Cassandra or DynamoDB offer flexible schemas or horizontal scalability for specific access patterns. The choice depends on data relationships, consistency needs and query patterns.

title: Normalization
text: Normalization organises tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies, for example 1NF removes repeating groups, 2NF removes partial dependencies and 3NF removes transitive dependencies. Denormalization is sometimes used deliberately to speed up reads.

title: PostgreSQL
text: PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database known for standards compliance, strong transactional guarantees, rich indexing (B-tree, GIN, GiST), JSONB support, and extensions such as pgvector for vector similarity search.

title: Redis and caching
text: Redis is an in-memory key-value store used for caching, rate limiting, sessions, queues and pub/sub. Caching reduces latency and load; the main challenges are invalidation, consistency and choosing appropriate expiry times.

title: MongoDB
text: MongoDB is a document database that stores JSON-like documents with flexible schemas. It suits data that is naturally hierarchical or varies in shape, supports secondary indexes and aggregation pipelines, and scales horizontally with sharding.

title: Scaling web systems
text: Systems scale vertically by using bigger machines or horizontally by adding instances behind a load balancer. Stateless services scale horizontally easily; state moves to databases, caches and queues. Read replicas, caching, sharding and asynchronous processing address database and throughput limits.

title: CAP theorem
text: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. In practice designers choose per use case, for example strong consistency for payments and eventual consistency for feeds or analytics.

title: Message queues
text: Message queues such as Kafka, RabbitMQ or SQS decouple producers from consumers, absorb traffic spikes and enable asynchronous processing and retries. Designs must consider delivery guarantees, ordering, idempotent consumers and dead-letter queues.

title: Microservices vs monolith
text: A monolith is simpler to build, test and deploy early on. Microservices allow independent deployment and scaling of components but add network calls, distributed data management, observability and operational complexity. Many teams start with a modular monolith.

title: Rate limiting
text: Rate limiting protects services from abuse and overload. Common algorithms are fixed window, sliding window and token bucket, typically enforced at an API gateway or with a shared store such as Redis so limits hold across instances.

title: System design interview approach
text: A structured system design answer clarifies functional and non-functional requirements, estimates scale, proposes a high-level architecture, walks through data flow and storage, then discusses scaling, reliability, security and trade-offs.

title: Logistic regression
text: Logistic regression is a linear classifier that models the probability of a class with the sigmoid function and is trained by minimising cross-entropy loss. It is fast, interpretable and a strong baseline for text classification when combined with TF-IDF features.

title: TF-IDF
text: TF-IDF weights a term by how often it appears in a document and down-weights terms that are common across the corpus. It turns text into sparse vectors for classical models such as logistic regression or SVMs.

title: Overfitting and regularisation
text: Overfitting happens when a model fits noise in the training data and generalises poorly. Remedies include more data, regularisation such as L1 or L2 penalties, dropout, early stopping, simpler models and cross-validation for model selection.

title: Bias-variance trade-off
text: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions, variance is error from sensitivity to the training data. Increasing model complexity usually lowers bias and raises variance; good models balance the two.

title: Classification metrics
text: Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced data. Precision measures how many predicted positives are correct, recall measures how many actual positives were found, and F1 is their harmonic mean. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC summarise performance across thresholds.

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
text: Gradient boosting builds an ensemble of shallow decision trees sequentially, each fitting the residual errors of the previous ones. XGBoost adds regularisation and efficient implementation, and is a strong choice for tabular data such as churn prediction.

title: Cross-validation
text: K-fold cross-validation splits data into k folds and trains k models, each validated on a different fold, giving a more reliable estimate of generalisation than a single split. Stratified folds preserve class proportions.

title: Gradient descent
text: Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction that reduces the loss, scaled by a learning rate. Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent and adaptive optimisers like Adam are standard for training neural networks.

title: Convolutional neural networks
text: CNNs apply learned convolution filters that detect local patterns such as edges and textures, with pooling to build translation-tolerant hierarchical features. They are widely used for image classification and detection.

title: Time and space complexity
text: Big-O notation describes how running time or memory grows with input size. Common classes are O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n^2). Interview answers should state the complexity of the proposed approach and discuss whether it can be improved.

title: Hash maps
text: Hash maps give average O(1) insertion and lookup by hashing keys into buckets. They are the standard tool for counting, deduplication and two-sum style problems; worst-case performance degrades with many collisions.

title: Binary search
text: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search range. It also applies to searching over an answer space when a monotonic condition exists.

title: Two pointers and sliding window
text: Two pointers and sliding windows solve many array and string problems in linear time by moving indices instead of using nested loops, for example finding pairs in a sorted array or the longest substring without repeating characters.

title: Dynamic programming
text: Dynamic programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by storing sub-results, either top-down with memoisation or bottom-up with a table. Defining the state and transition is the key step.

title: Graph traversal
text: Breadth-first search explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first search explores deeply and is used for connectivity, cycle detection and topological sort. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths with non-negative weights.

title: Object-oriented programming
text: The core OOP principles are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Good designs favour composition over deep inheritance and follow principles like single responsibility.

title: Python concurrency
text: In CPython the global interpreter lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads help I/O-bound work but not CPU-bound work. asyncio handles many concurrent I/O operations in one thread; multiprocessing parallelises CPU-bound work.

title: Web application security basics
text: Key web security practices include validating input, using parameterised queries against SQL injection, escaping output against XSS, protecting state-changing requests against CSRF, hashing passwords with bcrypt or argon2, enforcing authorisation on every request, and keeping secrets out of client code.

title: Authentication with tokens
text: Token-based authentication issues a signed token such as a JWT after login. Tokens should be short-lived, transmitted over HTTPS, stored in httpOnly cookies or secure storage, and validated for signature and expiry on every request.

title: STAR method
text: The STAR method structures behavioural answers as Situation, Task, Action and Result. Strong answers focus on the candidate's own actions, are specific, and end with a measurable or clearly described outcome and what was learned.

title: Answering strengths and weaknesses
text: For strengths, give one or two specific strengths with evidence. For weaknesses, name a real but non-critical weakness and explain concrete steps you are taking to improve it.

title: LLM latency optimisation
text: LLM application latency is reduced with token streaming, prompt caching, smaller context windows through retrieval, parallel retrieval calls, caching embeddings and choosing an appropriate model and effort level for each step.

title: LLM agents
text: An LLM agent uses a model to decide which tools or steps to run in a loop. Agent designs add flexibility but also cost, latency and failure modes, so production systems often use deterministic workflows and call the model only where judgement is required.
